Shadows at Noon

Why is a shadow shorter at noon?

Where shall we look?

01How can we save a shadow’s length?↗02Why is the noon shadow so short?↗03Which way does a shadow point?↗04What clue can a short shadow give us?↗

How can we save a shadow’s length?

Little puts a chalk mark at the long shadow’s tip.

A little explanation & something to try

A shadow forms where an object blocks sunlight. Mark its tip, then measure from the standing stick to the mark. Use the same measuring stick and unit to compare both lengths.

Try this. With Big, measure from the stick’s base to its shadow tip. Keep your eyes on the ground; never look at the sun.

Why is the noon shadow so short?

The same standing stick now has a short, crisp shadow.

A little explanation & something to try

Around noon, the sun is near its highest point in the sky for the day. Light reaches the ground from higher above, so the stick’s shadow stays closer to its base. A lower morning or afternoon sun makes a longer shadow.

Try this. Compare the short shadow with the earlier chalk mark.

Which way does a shadow point?

One side of the stick is bright. The shadow is on the other side.

A little explanation & something to try

The bright side faces the sun. The stick blocks some sunlight, leaving a shadow that points away from the light. Follow the shadow along the ground.

Try this. Point from the bright side, past the stick, toward the shadow.

What clue can a short shadow give us?

Little keeps a long line and a short line in the notebook.

A little explanation & something to try

A short noon shadow is a clue that the sun is high. Compare the same standing stick in the same place, using the same unit. Chalk marks and notes help us remember what changed. Measuring can lead to another question.

Try this. Ask one new question about tomorrow’s shadow.

The shadow that changed

Shadows at Noon

A morning question

Little Wonderer found a long shape beside a standing stick. It was a shadow: a place where the stick blocked sunlight, the light from the sun. “Will it stay this long?” Little asked. Big set a linen notebook beside the garden path. They had a question to keep.

What made the shadow?

Save the tip

Little took a piece of chalk, a soft stick for making marks. “First mark the tip,” said Big. Little drew a small line where the shadow ended. To measure is to find how long something is. They used a measuring stick from the wooden stick’s base to the chalk.

Why did Little mark the tip?

A smaller patch

At noon, the middle of the day, they came back. The wooden stick had stayed in place, but its shadow had changed. “It is short and crisp!” said Little. Around noon, the sun is near its highest point for the day. The morning shadow had reached much farther.

What changed between morning and noon?

Follow the light

“Which way does it point?” asked Big. Little studied the ground. Sunlight reached one side of the stick. The shadow stretched away on the other side. The bright side faced the sun; the shadow pointed away from the light. Little traced its edge along the ground with one finger.

Which way does a shadow point?

Compare the marks

Little marked the new tip with chalk. They used the same measuring stick to check both lengths. They began at the same standing stick and used the same unit each time. The noon length was shorter. “The stick stayed the same,” Little said. “The sun’s height changed.”

Why use the same unit each time?

A clue to keep

In the notebook, Little drew a long line for morning and a short line for noon. Later, when the sun was lower, the shadow would grow longer again. A short noon shadow was a clue to a high sun. “What will we notice tomorrow?” Little asked.

What could Little compare tomorrow?

A stick, sunlight, and a shadow

A clue worth keeping

Welcome words, pointing, or a sketch. Tell how a high sun makes a short shadow, and how you compared the lengths.

Follow a shadow through the day

  1. Predict. Will the same standing stick have a longer or shorter shadow around noon?
  2. Arrange in words. Stand a stick on level ground. Keep it in the same place. Choose a lower sun or a high noon sun.
  3. Activate. Sunlight reaches one side of the stick. The shadow points away from the light.
  4. Notice. The higher sun makes a short, crisp shadow. A lower morning or afternoon sun makes a longer shadow. Mark each tip with chalk, then compare lengths using the same unit.

A short noon shadow is a clue that the sun is high. Study the ground and keep a question.

Quiz

1. In this sunny yard, what happens to the same stick’s shadow around noon?

2. What happens to the shadow when the sun is lower?

3. Which way does a shadow point?

4. How can Little compare morning and noon shadows?

Answer key
Quiz 1
Around noon, the sun is near its highest point for the day, so the same standing stick has a shorter shadow.
Quiz 2
A lower sun makes a longer shadow from the same standing stick.
Quiz 3
A shadow points away from the light. The bright side of the stick faces the sun.
Quiz 4
Keep the stick standing in the same place. Mark each tip and measure from the stick with the same unit, then compare the lengths.

Small discoveries. Time together.

For grown-ups

Age 8, Grade 3 reading, and Grade 2 math. This story uses a sunny yard at middle latitudes. Solar noon is when the sun reaches its highest point that day; it need not be 12:00 by the clock. For the same vertical stick on level ground, that gives the shortest daytime shadow. The sun’s height varies with place and season; in Illinois it is never directly overhead. Clear sunlight gives a distinct edge; clouds can soften it. The diorama isolates sun height and light direction, with equal chalk spaces for comparison, not a clock or local forecast. The math counts equal groups and rows of garden and notebook objects. For an optional outdoor try, an adult helps place a stable blunt stick beside a path. Enjoy watching the shadow on the ground; never look at the sun.

Age 8 / Grade 3 reading. Welcome shared reading, spoken answers, and dictation. Pause at noon, shadow, measure, chalk, stick, and sunlight.

About the pictures and numbers. Pictures are imagined, enlarged illustrations, not photographs or measurements. Math numbers are made up for the story.

Illustration explanations: NOAA · solar noon and a standing stick · NASA · the noon sun and the seasons
